name: Madhaveswari Shakti Peetha (Alopi Devi Temple), Prayagraj
deity: The Goddess as Madhaveswari (Lalita), worshipped here as Alopi Devi or Alop Shankari in the form of a sacred palanquin; Bhairava as Bhava
period: Ancient Shakta tirtha of Prayaga, named in the Ashtadasha Shakti Peetha stotram; the present shrine at Alopibagh has no documented founding date, with Maratha-era patronage of Prayag's temples
dynasty: Founding not documented; Maratha (Scindia) patronage of Prayag's shrines and ghats
summary: Near the Sangam of the Ganga and Yamuna, the Prayaga Peetha honours the Goddess as Madhaveswari; in popular worship it is identified with the Alopi Devi temple, where a wooden palanquin rather than an image is venerated, though sources differ on the exact shrine.

sections.history: Prayaga, today's Prayagraj, is one of the oldest pilgrim sites of India, where the Ganga and Yamuna meet and the lost Sarasvati is believed to join them unseen. In the Ashtadasha Shakti Peetha stotram attributed to Adi Shankara the verse names it 'Prayage Madhaveswari'. Which shrine in the city is that Peetha is not settled. Popular tradition and many guides identify it with the Alopi Devi temple in Alopibagh, also called Alop Shankari, Lalita or Madhaveswari. Other sources point instead to the Lalita Devi temple at Meerapur on the Yamuna bank, and some name Kalyani Devi. No dated record of the Alopi temple's founding has been found. The Maratha chief Mahadji Shinde, who developed the Sangam area during his stay in 1771 and 1772, and later Baiza Bai Scindia, who renovated its ghats and temples, are remembered as patrons of Prayag, and the shrine has been kept in worship through the centuries.
sections.architecture: The temple is a modest, much-visited shrine in the old quarter of the city, and its character lies in what it leaves out. There is no sculpted image of the goddess in the sanctum. Instead a wooden palanquin, the doli, hangs above a small pool of water, and it is this that devotees worship as the presence of the Mother. The sanctum and its surroundings follow the North Indian temple tradition, simple and functional rather than monumental, and the daily crowds of pilgrims give the courtyard its energy. Visitors who expect carved halls will find a different kind of sacredness, one of absence and water, in keeping with the meaning of the name Alopi, the one who vanished.
sections.legends: The Peetha tradition belongs to the story of Sati. After her death at Daksha's sacrifice, Shiva bore her body across the world, and Vishnu's discus scattered it, and where each part fell a Shakti Peetha arose. The Peetha Nirnaya Tantra places her fingers at Prayaga, with the goddess as Lalita and Bhairava as Bhava. At Alopi, devotees say, a part of her hand fell into the pond and vanished without trace, which gave the shrine its name and explains why no image is kept. A local oral account tells instead of a bride, carried in her palanquin through a forest of robbers, who disappeared from it as the bandits attacked, leaving only the doli. Either way, the empty palanquin is the sign of the Goddess who is present yet unseen.
sections.festivals: Navratri, in both the spring and autumn cycles, is the temple's main season, when the nine forms of the goddess are worshipped for nine days and a fair gathers around the shrine. Dussehra is also observed with devotion. Devotees tie a sacred thread, the raksha sutra, on the wrist as they make their wishes. During the Magh Mela and the great Kumbh, when millions bathe at the Sangam, the whole city fills with pilgrims and the temple receives visitors from far away. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the lunar calendar.
sections.experience: Come as a pilgrim to the Sangam and add this shrine to the day. It is a lively, close, devotional place rather than a quiet one, with chants, bells and offerings all around the courtyard, and the doli is approached with folded hands, not with a search for an image. Many pilgrims combine the visit with a boat to the confluence, the Akshayavat and Beni Madhava, and the Lalita Devi temple at Meerapur, so that the Goddess of Prayaga is honoured at more than one doorway. Avoid Navratri evenings and the Magh Mela and Kumbh dates unless you are prepared for dense crowds.

visit.timings: Commonly listed as open from morning to late evening, roughly 6 a.m. to 10 p.m., though sources give slightly different hours; confirm locally, especially during Navratri and the Magh Mela.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the temple.
visit.photography: Rules are set by the temple, and photography is generally not welcome at the sanctum itself. Look for posted notices and ask before photographing the doli, rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The temple stands in Alopibagh in the old city of Prayagraj, a few kilometres from the Sangam and, by one listing, about 3.5 km from Prayagraj Junction, the city's main railway station. Prayagraj also has an airport. Auto-rickshaws and cabs serve the area, though riverfront and temple roads are often closed or congested during the Magh Mela and Kumbh.
